{{nihongo|'''Ikuta Shrine'''|生田神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Settsu Province]].

'''Ikuta Shrine''' (いくたじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|abstract|Q845945|ar|جينجا|arz|ضريح شنتو|bcl|Shinto shrine|ca|Jinja|cs|Šintoistická svatyně|da|Shinto-tempel|de|Shintō-Schrein|el|Σιντοϊστικό Ιερό|eo|Ŝintoa sanktejo|es|Jinja|eu|Jinja|fa|معبد شینتویی|fi|Šintolainen pyhäkkö|fr|Sanctuaire shinto|hi|शिंतो मंदिर|hr|Šintoistički hram|hu|Sintó szentély|id|Jinja|it|Jinja|ja|神社|ka|ძინძია|ko|신사 (신토)|lb|Shintō-Schräin|mr|शिंतो मंदिर|nl|Jinja (heiligdom)|no|Jinja|or|ଜିଞ୍ଜା|pl|Jinja|pt|Templo xintoísta|ru|Дзиндзя|sc|Jinja|simple|Shinto shrine|sl|Šintoistično svetišče|sr|Шинтоистички храм|sv|Jinja|th|ศาลเจ้าชินโต|tok|tomo sewi pi nasin sewi Sinto|tr|Şinto tapınağı|uk|Святилище (синто)|uz|Dzindzya|vi|Thần xã|wuu|神社|zh|神社|zh_yue|神社|qid=Q845945}} located in {{ill|Chūō-ku, Kobe|Q686802|qid=Q686802|lt=Chūō Ward}}, {{ill|Kobe|Q48320|qid=Q48320}}, {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|Q130290|qid=Q130290}}. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}} ({{ill|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964}}), and under the {{ill|Q712534|lt=former shrine ranking system}} it was classified as a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kanpei-chūsha}}. Along with {{ill|Hirota Shrine (Osaka City)|Q1466105|qid=Q1466105}} and {{ill|Nagata Shrine|Q661395|qid=Q661395}}, it is a shrine with a history dating back to {{ill|Empress Jingū|Q232803|qid=Q232803}}, and together with Nagata Shrine and {{ill|Minatogawa Shrine|Q713188|qid=Q713188}} it is one of the representative shrines of Kobe. In the past, the area that is now central Kobe City was shrine land, which became the origin of the place name “Kobe.” Locally, it is affectionately known as “Ikuta-san.”

=== Enshrined Deity ===
* Main enshrined deity – {{ill|Wakahiru-me|ja|稚日女尊|zh|稚日女尊|qid=Q11596349}} (わかひるめのみこと)<ref name="d-10">{{Cite web |url=https://www.city.kobe.lg.jp/documents/44019/d-10_ikutajinja.pdf |title=History of Chūō Ward: Historic Sites and Place Names – Ikuta Shrine|access-date=2024-11-30|publisher=Kobe City}}</ref>. The name means “the young and fresh sun goddess,” and she is said to be either the childhood name or the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=nigi-mitama}} (gentle spirit) of {{ill|Amaterasu|Q455602|qid=Q455602}}, or her younger sister deity.

=== History ===
According to the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ar|نيهون شوكي|as|নিহন শ্ব'কি|az|Nihon şoki|bcl|Nihon Shoki|bg|Нихоншоки|ca|Nihon Shoki|cs|Nihonšoki|de|Nihonshoki|el|Νιχόν Σόκι|eo|Nihon Ŝoki|es|Nihonshoki|eu|Nihon Shoki|fa|نیهون شوکی|fi|Nihonshoki|fr|Nihon shoki|gl|Nihon Shoki|he|ניהון שוקי|hi|निहोन शोकी|hr|Nihon Shoki|hu|Nihonsoki|id|Nihon Shoki|it|Nihon shoki|ja|日本書紀|jv|Nihon Shoki|ko|일본서기|la|Nihon Shoki|mk|Нихон шоки|ms|Nihon Shoki|my|နိဟွန်းရှောခိ|nl|Nihon Shoki|no|Nihonshoki|oc|Nihon shoki|pl|Nihon-shoki|pt|Nihon Shoki|rsk|Нихон Шоки|ru|Нихон сёки|sco|Nihon Shoki|sh|Nihon Shoki|simple|Nihon Shoki|sl|Nihon Šoki|sq|Nihon Shoki|sr|Нихон шоки|sv|Nihonshoki|ta|நிஹான் ஷோகி|th|นิฮงโชกิ|tl|Nihon Shoki|tr|Nihon Shoki|uk|Ніхон Сьокі|uz|Nihon shoki|vi|Nhật Bản thư kỷ|zh|日本書紀|zh_min_nan|Ji̍t-pún Su-kì|zh_yue|日本書紀|qid=Q813935}}, in the first year of {{ill|Empress Jingū|Q232803|qid=Q232803}} ({{ill|201|Q30387|qid=Q30387}}), while the Empress was returning after completing the {{ill|Three Han Campaign|Q11249435|qid=Q11249435}}, her ship stopped moving at what is now {{ill|Port of Kobe|Q1336906|qid=Q1336906}}. She performed divination, whereupon {{ill|Wakahiru-me|ja|稚日女尊|zh|稚日女尊|qid=Q11596349}} appeared and delivered an oracle saying, “I wish to dwell in the land of Ikuta Nagasa. Command {{ill|Unagami no Isachi|Q11558664|qid=Q11558664}} to enshrine me in the land of Ikuta.” The Empress then appointed Unagami no Isachi as priest and had Wakahirume no Mikoto enshrined at {{ill|Mount Nunobiki|Q11480792|qid=Q11480792}} (Sand Mountain), located behind the present {{ill|Shin-Kōbe Station|Q801435|qid=Q801435}}. This is said to be the beginning of the shrine<ref name="由緒">[https://ikutajinja.or.jp/history Ikuta Shrine official website – History]</ref>.

Although the shrine was originally on Sand Mountain, on April 9 of {{ill|Enryaku|Q1373176|qid=Q1373176}} 18 ({{ill|799|Q33488|qid=Q33488}}), a massive flood of {{ill|Nunobiki Falls|Q3695449|qid=Q3695449}} caused the western edge of the mountain to collapse, damaging and tilting the shrine buildings. Tōne Shichidayū of Ikuta Village evacuated the sacred object and, carrying it on his back, searched for a new site for seven or eight days. When he reached Ikuta Forest, the sacred object suddenly became too heavy to carry further. Believing this to be the deity’s will, he enshrined it there—at the present location<ref name="由緒"/>.

In the first year of {{ill|Daidō|de|Daidō (Ära)|es|Daidō|fa|دایدو (دوره)|fr|Ère Daidō|ia|Daido|id|Daidō|ja|大同 (日本)|ko|다이도 (일본)|ru|Дайдо (нэнго)|simple|Daidō|sr|Даидо|th|ไดโด|tr|Daidō|uk|Дайдо|zh|大同 (日本)|zh_yue|大同 (日本)|qid=Q1373191|lt=Daidō}} ({{ill|806|ab|806|af|806|als|806|am|806 እ.ኤ.አ.|an|806|ar|806|ary|806|ast|806|az|806|azb|۸۰۶ (میلادی)|bar|806|bcl|806|be|806|be_x_old|806|bg|806|bn|৮০৬|bpy|মারি ৮০৬|br|806|bs|806.|ca|806|cdo|806 nièng|ceb|806|ckb|٨٠٦|crh|806|cs|806|csb|806|cv|806|cy|806|da|806|de|806|el|806|eml|806|eo|806|es|806|et|806|eu|806|fa|۸۰۶ (میلادی)|fi|806|fo|806|fr|806|frr|806|fy|806|ga|806|gan|806年|gd|806|gl|806|he|806|hi|806|hr|806.|ht|806 (almanak jilyen)|hu|806|hy|806|id|806|ilo|806|io|806|is|806|it|806|ja|806年|jv|806|ka|806|kaa|806|kk|806 жыл|ko|806년|la|806|lb|806|lij|806|lmo|806|lt|806 m.|lv|806. gads|map_bms|806|mdf|806|mg|806|mhr|806|mk|806|mr|इ.स. ८०६|mrj|806 и|ms|806|mzn|۸۰۶|nah|806|nap|806|nds|806|new|सन् ८०६|nl|806|nn|806|no|806|nrm|806|nso|806|oc|806|or|୮୦୬|os|806-æм аз|pl|806|pt|806|qu|806|ro|806|ru|806 год|rue|806|sa|८०६|scn|806|sd|806ع|se|806|sh|806.|shn|806|si|806|sk|806|sl|806|smn|806|sq|806|sr|806|su|806|sv|806|sw|806|tg|Соли 806|th|พ.ศ. 1349|tk|806|tl|806|tly|806|tr|806|tt|806 ел|uk|806|ur|806ء|uz|806|vec|806|vi|806|vls|806|war|806|wuu|806年|xmf|806|zh|806年|zh_min_nan|806 nî|zh_yue|806年|qid=Q30021}}), the imperial court granted the shrine 44 households known as “Ikuta no Shinpu Yonjuuyonko,” households that provided offerings, care, and protection—{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kobe}}. Since then, the area of present-day central Kobe City became shrine land. It is said that this “Kanbe” later changed to “Konbe,” and eventually came to be called “Kōbe,” forming the place name Kobe<ref name="d-10" /><ref name="由緒"/>.

In the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}, it is listed as “Ikuta Shrine, Yabe District, {{ill|Settsu Province|ca|Província de Settsu|cs|Provincie Seccu|de|Provinz Settsu|eo|Provinco Seccu|es|Provincia de Settsu|fa|ولایت ستسو|fr|Province de Settsu|gl|Provincia de Settsu|hak|Settsu-koet|id|Provinsi Settsu|it|Settsu (provincia)|ja|摂津国|ko|셋쓰국|lt|Seccu žemė|nl|Settsu (provincie)|pt|Província de Settsu|ru|Сэтцу (провинция)|simple|Settsu Province|sk|Seccu (provincia)|sr|Провинција Сецу|tr|Settsu (vilayet)|uk|Провінція Сеццу|zh|攝津國|zh_min_nan|Settu-kok|zh_yue|攝津國|qid=Q864163}},” ranked as a {{ill|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964}}, and noted as receiving offerings at the Tsukinami, Aname, and Niiname festivals.

During the late {{ill|Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292}}, in the {{ill|Battle of Ichi-no-Tani|Q2116658|qid=Q2116658}} fought in February of {{ill|Juei|Q598057|qid=Q598057}} 3 ({{ill|1184|Q19728|qid=Q19728}}), {{ill|Taira no Tomomori|Q736706|qid=Q736706}} established his main camp in Ikuta Forest<ref name="境内を歩く">[https://ikutajinja.or.jp/precinct Ikuta Shrine official website – Walking the Grounds]</ref>.

Under the {{ill|Q712534|lt=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}, the shrine was designated a prefectural shrine in {{ill|1871|Q7746|qid=Q7746}} ({{ill|Meiji era|ar|فترة مييجي|ast|Dómina Meiji|az|Meydzi dövrü|azb|مئی‌جی دؤورو|be|Перыяд Мэйдзі|bn|মেইজি যুগ|bo|མེའི་ཇིའི་དུས་དུས་མཚམས།|ca|Era Meiji|cs|Období Meidži|da|Meiji-perioden|de|Meiji-Zeit|el|Μεϊτζί (περίοδος)|es|Era Meiji|et|Meiji periood|eu|Meiji Aroa|fa|دوره میجی|fi|Meiji-kausi|fr|Ère Meiji|gl|Período Meiji|he|תקופת מייג'י|hr|Meiji (razdoblje)|ht|Epòk Meiji|hu|Meidzsi-kor|id|Zaman Meiji|io|Ero Meiji|is|Meiji-tímabilið|it|Periodo Meiji|ja|明治|ka|მეიძის ეპოქა|kbp|Mejii wɛɛ yaa alɩwaatʊ|kk|Мэйдзи дәуірі|ko|메이지 시대|la|Aetas Meiji|lt|Meidži laikotarpis|lv|Meidzi periods|mk|Меиџи (период)|mn|Мэйжийн эрин|ms|Zaman Meiji|nl|Meijiperiode|nn|Meiji|no|Meiji-perioden|pl|Meiji (okres)|pt|Era Meiji|ro|Perioada Meiji|ru|Мэйдзи|simple|Meiji period|sk|Obdobie Meidži|sq|Periudha Meixhi|sr|Меиџи период|sv|Meijiperioden|ta|மெய்சி காலம்|th|ยุคเมจิ|tl|Panahong Meiji|tr|Meiji Dönemi|uk|Період Мейдзі|ur|میجی دور|vi|Thời kỳ Minh Trị|war|Panahon Meiji|wuu|明治|zh|明治|zh_classical|明治|zh_min_nan|Bêng-tī|zh_yue|明治|qid=Q3125096}} 4). Later, during the western imperial tour of {{ill|Emperor Meiji|Q174231|qid=Q174231}} in {{ill|1885|Q7821|qid=Q7821}} (Meiji 18), it was promoted to a Kanpei shrine, becoming a Kanpei-shōsha, and in {{ill|1896|Q7846|qid=Q7846}} (Meiji 29) it was further elevated to {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kanpei-chūsha}}.

The shrine buildings were damaged in the {{ill|1938|Q18645|qid=Q18645}} ({{ill|Shōwa era|Q327567|qid=Q327567}} 13) {{ill|1938 Hanshin flood|Q11656935|qid=Q11656935|lt=Kobe Flood}}, destroyed by fire in the {{ill|Bombing of Kobe in World War II|Q4940711|qid=Q4940711}} on March 17, {{ill|1945|Q5240|qid=Q5240}} (Shōwa 20), and damaged again in the {{ill|Damage by Great Hanshin earthquake|Q11392882|qid=Q11392882}} of {{ill|1995|Q2068|qid=Q2068}} ({{ill|Heisei era|Q234510|qid=Q234510}} 7). Each time, it was rebuilt, leading to reverence for the shrine as that of a “reviving deity.”

In January {{ill|2000|Q1985|qid=Q1985}} (Heisei 12), a “Ikuta Shrine Earthquake Reconstruction Monument” was erected on the west side of the main hall, with a waterproof pump installed behind it to draw water from the pond<ref name="d-10" />.

Within the grounds are a monument to the Noh chant “Ikuta Atsumori,” a knife mound donated by local restaurants and food-related companies, and a sacred camphor tree ({{ill|Camphora officinarum|Q158722|qid=Q158722|lt=kusunoki}}). Many donor names written on the pillars belong to hotel or maritime-related companies.

=== Court Ranks ===

=== Legends and Traditions ===
During the great flood of Enryaku 18 (799), pine trees ({{ill|Pine|Q12024|qid=Q12024|lt=matsu}}) had been planted around the shrine, but they were said to have been completely ineffective in preventing the flood. As a result, pines came to be disliked, and at New Year, cedar decorations are erected instead of {{ill|Kadomatsu|Q2667233|qid=Q2667233}}<ref name="d-10" />. It is also said that not a single pine tree is planted in Ikuta Forest<ref name="d-10" />.

Near {{ill|Kumochi-chō|Q11567845|qid=Q11567845}} in Chūō Ward, close to {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kumochi Hachiman Shrine}}, there is a torii known as the “Asahi Torii”<ref name="hyogo-jinjacho_komochihachiman">{{Cite web|ja|url=http://www.hyogo-jinjacho.com/data/6301039.html|title=Kumochi Hachiman Shrine|publisher={{ill|Hyogo Prefectural Shrine Association|Q135249839|qid=Q135249839}}|accessdate=2020-07-10}}</ref>, which is said to have been the first torii when Ikuta Shrine was located on Sand Mountain. It is called the “Asahi Torii” because it is said not to cast a shadow even when struck by the morning sun on New Year’s Day<ref name="hyogo-jinjacho_komochihachiman"/>.

The chief priest Takahisa Katō’s book *Ikuta Shrine* ({{ill|Gakuseisha|Q11448819|qid=Q11448819}}, 2005) provides a detailed explanation including its history.

In the Noh play *Ikuta Atsumori*, the surviving child of {{ill|Taira no Atsumori|Q2284163|qid=Q2284163|lt=Atsumori}} encounters his deceased father here through prayers made to {{ill|Shimogamo Shrine|Q701620|qid=Q701620|lt=Kamo Myōjin}}.

=== Auxiliary Shrines ===
The following {{ill|Setsumatsusha|Q1071160|qid=Q1071160}} are located within the grounds<ref name="ikutajinja-keidai">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://ikutajinja.or.jp/precinct|title=Walking the Grounds – Shrine Edition|publisher=Ikuta Shrine|accessdate=2020-07-10}}</ref>. The enshrined deities and descriptions are according to the official website<ref name="ikutajinja-keidai"/>.
* {{ill|Sumiyoshi Shrine|Q11381857|qid=Q11381857}} – Deities: {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Uwatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Nakatsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Sokotsutsu-no-O-no-Mikoto}}. Deities of maritime and traffic safety.
* {{ill|Hachiman shrine|fa|معبد هاچیمان|fr|Sanctuaire Hachiman|it|Santuario di Hachiman|ja|八幡宮|simple|Hachiman shrines|vi|Đền thờ thần Hachiman|zh|八幡宮|qid=Q11390939|lt=Hachiman Shrine}} – Deity: {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|Q317997|qid=Q317997}}. Deity of warding off misfortune and bringing good fortune.
* {{ill|Suwa Shrine|Q2370082|qid=Q2370082}} – Deity: {{ill|Takeminakata|qid=Q9150391|lt=Takeminakata-no-Mikoto|qid=Q9150391}}. Deity of agriculture, hunting, martial fortune, and strength.
* {{ill|Hiyoshi Shrine|Q11505065|qid=Q11505065}} – Deity: {{ill|Oyamakui no Kami|qid=Q10935105|lt=Ōyamakui-no-Mikoto}}. Deity of agriculture, industry, and abundant harvests.
* {{ill|Ichikishima Shrines|Q11480540|qid=Q11480540}} – Deity: {{ill|Ichikishima-hime|fr|Ichikishimahime|ja|イチキシマヒメ|simple|Ichikishima-hime|zh|市寸島比賣命|qid=Q11059454|lt=Ichikishimahime-no-Mikoto}}. Deity of performing arts and water.
* {{ill|Inari shrine|Q514480|qid=Q514480}} – Deity: {{ill|Ukanomitama|lt=Ukanomitama|Q3080728|qid=Q3080728|qid=Q3080728|lt=Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto}}. Deity of livelihood protection, food, and rice.
* Sai Shrine – Deities: {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Chigaeshi no Ōkami}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Yachimatahiko-no-Kami}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Yachimatahime-no-Kami}}. Deities of disease prevention and road protection.
* Ikazuchi Daijin Shrine – Deity: {{ill|Nakatomi no Ikatsu|Q55536814|qid=Q55536814|lt=Nakatomi Ikatsu no Muraji}}. Ancestral deity of the Gokō family, former shrine priests.
* Hitomaro Shrine – Deity: {{ill|Kakinomoto no Hitomaro|Q380818|qid=Q380818|lt=Kakinomoto no Hitomaro}}. Deity of marital harmony and academic achievement.
* Ebisu Shrine – Deity: {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ebisu-no-Mikoto}}. Deity of business prosperity.
* Ōumi Shrine – Deity: {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Sarutahiko-no-Mikoto}}. Deity of maritime safety, traffic safety, direction warding, and path opening.
* {{ill|Matsuo shrine|Q11529677|qid=Q11529677}} – Deity: {{ill|Oyamakui no Kami|qid=Q10935105|lt=Ōyamakui-no-Mikoto}}. Deity of sake brewing and agriculture/industry. A monument designates Ikuta Shrine as the “birthplace of {{ill|Nada-Gogō|Q6957369|qid=Q6957369}} sake brewing,” and the {{ill|Sacred fences|es|Tamagaki|fi|Tamagaki|fr|Tamagaki|ja|玉垣|qid=Q3078312}} fence was maintained by sake brewers and merchants<ref name="hasshonochi-nadagogo">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://840.gnpp.jp/nadagogoshuzo/|title=Birthplace of Nada Gogo Sake Brewing|work=Birthplace Collection|date=2018-3|accessdate=2020-07-10}}</ref>. The monument records that, according to the {{ill|Engishiki|ar|إنجيشيكي (كتاب ياباني)|de|Engishiki|es|Engishiki|fr|Engishiki|he|אנגישיקי|id|Engishiki|it|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|ko|엔기시키|min|Engishiki|mr|इंगिशिकी|nl|Engishiki|pt|Engishiki|ru|Энгисики|simple|Engishiki|tr|Engishiki|uk|Енґісікі|zh|延喜式|qid=Q1342448}} “{{ill|Genba-ryō|Q11572314|qid=Q11572314}},” when entertaining envoys from Silla at {{ill|Minume Shrine|Q11499217|qid=Q11499217|lt=Minume Port}}, rice was gathered from Ikuta Shrine, {{ill|Hirota Shrine (Osaka City)|Q1466105|qid=Q1466105}}, {{ill|Nagata Shrine|Q661395|qid=Q661395}}, and {{ill|Kataoka Shrine (Oji Town)|Q43594918|qid=Q43594918|lt=Kataoka Shrine}} in Yamato Province, and new sake brewed at Ikuta Shrine was to be used<ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=https://jp.sake-times.com/special/project/pr_tatenokawa_004|title=Was the origin of “Nada no Ki-Ippon” a divine oracle?! – The connection between Nada sake and three shrines|work=SAKETIMES|date=2019-02-21|accessdate=2020-07-10}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|ja|url=http://www.archives.city.amagasaki.hyogo.jp/chronicles/visual/01kodai/kodai1-3.html|title=The Yamato polity and the Ina River basin|work=Illustrated History of Amagasaki (Web Edition)|accessdate=2020-07-10}}</ref><ref name="hasshonochi-nadagogo"/>.
* Togakushi Shrine – Deity: {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Tajikarao-no-Mikoto}}. Deity of physical health, strength enhancement, and great power.
* Ikutamorizasusha – Deity: {{ill|Empress Jingū|Q232803|qid=Q232803}}. Deity of safe childbirth, growth of all things, and guardian of Ikuta Forest.

=== Ikuta Forest ===
Behind the main hall lies Ikuta Forest (Ikuta no Mori), which is said to have once extended as far as the banks of the old Ikuta River<ref name="d-10" />. The forest appears in *{{ill|The Pillow Book|Q615137|qid=Q615137}}*<ref name="d-10" />, and has been celebrated in many poems.
* “Even the autumn wind cannot fully blow before the colors change—beneath the dew, the grasses of Ikuta Forest” ({{ill|Fujiwara no Teika|Q378425|qid=Q378425}}, *Shoku Gosen Wakashū*)
* “In Ikuta Forest of Tsū Province, no one comes; through the night autumn wind, I speak to the moon” (Prince {{ill|Prince Munetaka|Q708897|qid=Q708897}}, *Shin Gosen Wakashū*, Volume 5, Autumn)

Because of its strategic position behind the Ikuta River, it was a battlefield during the {{ill|Battle of Ichi-no-Tani|Q2116658|qid=Q2116658}} of the Genpei War and the {{ill|Battle of Minatogawa|Q114620|qid=Q114620}} in the Nanboku-chō period<ref name="d-10" />.

=== Approach ===
The first torii stands at the southwestern end of Ikuta Road, southwest of {{ill|Kobe-Sannomiya Station|Q377926|qid=Q377926}}. From there, the approach passes through Center Street heading north, crosses Ikuta Shindō, and reaches the shrine name marker and second torii northeast of {{ill|Hands (store)|Q859212|qid=Q859212|lt=Hands}}. Upon entering the grounds, there is a paid parking area, beyond which stand the third torii and the sacred gate.
